intro: To request a shift swap with your charge nurse, send one short email that names both shifts, both nurses, and a reply-by time. Agree the trade with your coworker first, and keep patient details out of the message. Check your unit's rules before you send anything.
tldr: Agree the trade with your coworker before you email the charge nurse.
Name the date, both shift times, both nurses, and the unit in the email.
Ask for a yes or no by a set time, and say what happens if the answer is no.
Keep patient names, room numbers, and diagnoses out of the message.
Send overtime requests as their own email, because they ask for something different.

blocks.text: Why the email matters more than the swap

A swap is not real until the schedule shows it. Until then, you still own the shift. If your unit uses When I Work, the employee stays responsible for a swap or drop until a coworker picks up the shift. A vague email can leave you holding a shift you thought you had given away. The email is the record. It should answer the questions the charge nurse must answer anyway: who, which shift, which unit, and whether the hours still work.

Charge nurses manage staffing for a whole unit at once. They rarely have time to chase a half-written message. A clear request gets read once and answered. A fuzzy one brings three follow-up questions, and by then the window for a decision may have closed. Your goal is simple. Make the yes easy to give.

Scale explains why this comes up so often. The Bureau of Labor Statistics counts about 3.5 million registered nurse jobs in 2025. It says nurses in hospitals usually work in shifts to cover the clock. They may work nights, weekends, and holidays, and some are on call with short notice. Every swap touches a schedule that already has many moving parts.

The study with the clearest numbers on this is limited. In a 2022 survey of nurses at South Korean hospitals, 40.3% had worked mandatory overtime in the previous month. Among the factors studied, mandatory overtime was the only variable significantly linked to intent to leave. It was not linked to burnout in the same study. The sample was a convenience sample, so the figure is not a US number and does not show how common this is everywhere.
Template for a nurse shift swap request email

Start with a subject line that names the date, the shift, and the unit. Charge nurses scan inboxes between tasks, so the facts go first. A subject such as Shift swap request: Thursday night, Med-Surg East tells the reader what the message is before they open it. Keep the body short. Four or five lines usually cover it.

rows: Shift swap request, the date, the shift, and the unit
The change is visible before the email is opened
Date, start time, end time, and unit
Removes questions about which shift you mean
Their full name as the schedule shows it
Shows the trade has already been agreed
A specific time, such as the end of the day
Gives the charge nurse room to answer before the shift
What happens if the trade is refused
Makes a no easy to give
blocks.caption: Fields to fill in before you press send.

blocks.text: Here is a full draft you can paste into Outlook. Replace each bracket with your details. Keep the wording plain. Do not add apologies or long reasons.

items: I would like to swap my Thursday night shift with [coworker name].
[Coworker name] has agreed to take my shift, and I will take their Friday day shift.
Could you approve the swap in the schedule? Please reply by [time] on [day] so I can plan.
If the trade does not work, I will keep my original shift. Thank you, [your name]

blocks.text: Two details are easy to forget. Name the coworker the way the schedule spells their name. Also say what the trade covers, so the charge nurse does not have to guess. A swap trades two shifts. It is not a favor for one person.

blocks.title: Keep patient details out
blocks.text: Do not put patient names, room numbers, or diagnoses in the email. Follow your employer's rules for patient data. Your unit may also have its own channel for schedule changes, so check that before you send.
Overtime requests need a different ask

An overtime request is not a swap. A swap moves a shift from one person to another. Overtime adds hours to someone's week. That changes fatigue, coverage, and pay, so the charge nurse will weigh it differently. Say how many extra hours you can work, when you can start, and which unit you can cover. Phrase the ask as a question, not a demand.

Check the rules before you ask. The When I Work help articles do not say whether overtime shifts can be swapped. That depends on your employer's settings. Your unit might use a sign-up sheet, a manager list, or the scheduling app. Ask your scheduler which path applies before you send a message.
Worked example: a swap and an overtime ask

Say you are a staff nurse with a Thursday night shift. Your coworker, Sam, wants Friday off and offers a Friday day shift in trade. Before anyone writes to the charge nurse, you text Sam to confirm the trade. Sam agrees in writing. You open Outlook, press ⌘N for a new message, and paste the template.

This is a made-up example. The charge nurse replies that the trade works, with one condition. You must confirm it in the scheduling app by the end of the day. You open the When I Work web app in Chrome, go to My Schedule, and check the request status. If your manager has review turned on, the request sits in Pending Approval until someone approves it.

The overtime version reads differently. You write that you can pick up an extra day shift on Saturday, that you can start at seven a.m., and that you can cover the unit it needs. You ask whether overtime is open for Saturday and how it gets approved. You do not promise the hours until someone confirms them.
Where Lazur helps, and where it does not

Lazur can draft the email from what you tell it. It can also dictate text at your cursor. Hold fn, speak the message, and the text lands in the email. Then read every line before you send. Lazur does not press Send, change the schedule, or click buttons in your mail or scheduling app.

items: Draft: describe the swap out loud and get a clean email with placeholders to edit.
Dictate: hold fn in Outlook or Chrome and speak the message at the cursor.
Point: ask where the Send button is, and Lazur circles it on screen so you click it yourself.
Guide: ask for help in When I Work one click at a time. Lazur waits for each click.
Explain: ask what Pending Approval means on screen, and Lazur answers out loud.

blocks.text: Lazur does not know your unit's rules, your contract, or your employer's patient data policy. Use its draft as a starting point, then check it against your own policy. If you are unsure whether a detail belongs in the email, leave it out.
Mistakes that get swap requests refused

items: Sending the request before the coworker has agreed to the trade.
Leaving out a shift time, so the charge nurse has to ask what you mean.
Asking after the shift has started, or too close to the start.
Adding patient details to explain why you need the swap.
Forgetting to say what happens if the trade falls through.
Replying to a yes by text only, with no written record in the schedule.

blocks.text: Most of these come from one habit. The writer aims at their own needs instead of the charge nurse's questions. Read the email as someone who has never heard of you. If who, when, and what are missing, add them before you send.
After approval: confirm the schedule and your calendar

A yes in an email is not the same as a changed schedule. Open the When I Work web app and confirm the shift moved. If your manager must approve in Shift Requests, the approve or deny decision happens there. Users are notified automatically when a request is approved or denied.

Then update your own calendar. Add the new shift to Apple Calendar on your Mac, so your personal calendar matches the schedule. Save the template in Word too, so the next request starts from a draft you already trust.
For more on shift email in Outlook, see [Outlook for nurses on Mac](/for/nurses/outlook). For saving templates you can reuse, see [Word for nurses on Mac](/for/nurses/word).
Edge cases to check before you send

Some swaps fail for reasons the email cannot fix. Skill mix matters on many units, so a charge nurse may need a certain experience level on a shift. Certifications, orientation status, and float rules can also limit who may take a shift. Ask before you promise. A good email cannot override a policy.

New grads and nurses on orientation should check with a preceptor or manager first. Their approval may be needed for every change. Even if your unit lets you trade directly, the charge nurse can still decline.

If the answer is no, accept it without a fight. Thank the charge nurse, keep your original shift, and ask what would work next time. Denied requests notify the person who asked, but not the other people listed on the swap. Tell your coworker yourself.

faq.question: Should I email or text the charge nurse about a swap?
faq.answer: Agree the trade with your coworker by text first. Then use email for the written request, so there is a record. Some units use only the scheduling app for changes, so check which channel your unit uses before you rely on email.

faq.question: Is a shift swap the same as dropping a shift?
faq.answer: No. In When I Work, you can start a swap, a drop, or a release. You stay responsible for a swap or drop until a coworker picks up the shift. Choose the option that matches what you want before you start.

faq.question: What if the charge nurse does not reply?
faq.answer: Follow up once, with a short question, before the reply-by time. Do not assume silence means yes. Keep your original shift until you have an answer in writing or in the schedule.

faq.question: Can Lazur send the email for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur can draft the text and type it at your cursor when you dictate. You read it and press Send yourself. Lazur does not click buttons or operate your mail app for you.

faq.question: Do I need to give a reason for the swap?
faq.answer: It is up to you. A short, general reason, such as a family appointment, can help when a charge nurse must choose between requests. Never include patient information in the reason.

faq.question: Can I ask for a swap and overtime in the same email?
faq.answer: It is cleaner to send two emails. A swap changes who works a shift. An overtime request adds hours. Mixing them can confuse the charge nurse and delay both answers.

faq.question: Do these steps apply to every nurse?
faq.answer: The steps work for most staff nurses, but the rules change by employer, union, and state. Your employer's written policy and your manager's instructions come before anything on this page.

costs.title: Your shift does not move
costs.text: Until the swap is approved and the coworker picks up the shift, you are still responsible for it. A shared text is not enough. If the trade falls apart, you may end up working the shift you hoped to give away.

costs.title: Charge nurse time
costs.text: Each vague email costs the charge nurse time to decode. They must check the schedule, find both people, and reply with questions. Multiply that by every request in a week, and staffing decisions slow down for the whole unit.

costs.title: Goodwill with coworkers
costs.text: Missed handoffs and surprise changes make people less willing to help the next time. A clean request that is easy to say yes to builds goodwill. A messy one can cost you a favor you may need later.

costs.title: Overtime that wears you down
costs.text: Extra hours are not free. In the 2022 survey, mandatory overtime was the only variable the study found significantly linked to intent to leave, though it was not linked to burnout. Treat overtime as a real cost. Say no clearly when you need rest.

causes.title: Round-the-clock coverage
causes.text: Hospitals run shifts around the clock. The Bureau of Labor Statistics says nurses in hospitals usually work in shifts to provide that coverage. They may work nights, weekends, and holidays, and some are on call with short notice. Any change to one shift affects the people around it, so requests happen often.

causes.title: Mandatory overtime piles up
causes.text: In a 2022 survey of South Korean nurses, 40.3% had worked mandatory overtime in the previous month. That study is not US data. It still shows overtime is common enough to shape how people feel about staying in their jobs. Swap requests often follow a run of extra hours.

causes.title: Requests start in hallways and texts
causes.text: Many swaps start as a text or a quick word at the station. Without anything in writing, nobody can say who agreed to what. When the schedule is checked later, the change is missing, and the charge nurse has to sort it out under pressure.

causes.title: The ask is unclear
causes.text: A request such as Can we switch Thursday? leaves out the shift times, the unit, and the coworker. The charge nurse must ask several questions before deciding. Many people will not reply to those questions, so the request stalls and the shift stays with the wrong person.

causes.title: Approval steps people miss
causes.text: Some schedules need a manager's approval before a swap counts. In When I Work, a manager can turn on Require Manager Review for Swaps and Drops. That puts requests in Pending Approval until someone approves them, and it can delay when coworkers see the offer. If you do not know this, you may think the swap is done when it is not.

fixes.title: Agree with your coworker first
fixes.text: Ask the coworker to confirm the trade before you email anyone. A text is fine. Include both shift times and the date. If they back out, you have not made a request yet, and the charge nurse does not have to clean up after you.

fixes.title: Put the facts in the subject line
fixes.text: Put the date, the shift, and the unit in the subject line. For example: Shift swap request: Thursday night, Med-Surg East. The charge nurse can see the change without opening the email. Keep the body to one screen.

fixes.title: Use a four-part body
fixes.text: Open with the ask, then the two shifts, then the coworker's name, then the reply-by time. Four short parts beat one long paragraph. Read the draft once as the charge nurse would. If a question comes to mind, answer it in the email.

fixes.title: Set a reply-by time and a fallback
fixes.text: Pick a time that gives the charge nurse room to answer before the shift. Write it plainly, such as Reply by the end of the day. Add a fallback line: if this does not work, I will keep my shift. That removes pressure and makes a no easy to give.

fixes.title: Confirm in writing, then check the schedule
fixes.text: When you get a yes, reply with one line that restates the trade. Then check the schedule in the When I Work web app, or in the scheduling tool your unit uses. A yes in an inbox is not the same as a changed schedule.

fixes.title: Send overtime as a separate message
fixes.text: Write overtime requests as their own message. State the hours you can work, the start time, and the unit. Ask whether overtime is open and how it gets approved. Do not assume approval because you offered the hours.

plan.label: Before you ask
plan.title: Confirm the trade
plan.text: Talk to your coworker first. Agree on both shifts, the date, and who covers what. Confirm the trade in one text message, so you have a record before you write to the charge nurse.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: Draft and check the email
plan.text: Use the template and fill in the names and times. Read the email once as the charge nurse would. Check your unit's rules for swaps and overtime before you press Send.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: Send, then wait for the reply
plan.text: Send the email from Outlook and note the reply-by time. If the charge nurse has not answered by then, follow up once with a short, specific question.

plan.label: Day 3
plan.title: Confirm in the schedule
plan.text: Once the swap is approved, open the When I Work web app and check your shifts. Add the change to Apple Calendar on your Mac, so your week matches.

plan.label: Ongoing
plan.title: Save the template
plan.text: Keep the template in Word or in a Chrome bookmark. Update the wording after each request, so the next one takes minutes instead of an hour.
